title: Agricultural (Neolithic) revolution
summary: From about 12,000 years ago, people in at least eleven separate regions of the world began cultivating plants and herding animals, slowly turning wild species into crops and livestock and laying the economic foundation of villages, towns and states.
card: Farming was not invented once. In the Fertile Crescent, wild cereals were being managed by about 12,000 years ago, and similar transitions followed independently in China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes, the African Sahel and eastern North America. Each took thousands of years, and scholars still debate why it happened when it did and whether it made people's lives better or worse.
what:
The agricultural or Neolithic revolution is the shift, across many parts of the world, from living only on wild plants and animals to cultivating crops and keeping livestock. The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe introduced the idea of a prehistoric revolution in 1934 and popularised it in his 1936 book Man Makes Himself, picturing a single transformation that began with grain growing in Mesopotamia and spread outward.

Later evidence has replaced that picture with many separate beginnings. A 2014 review by Larson and 23 colleagues counts at least 11 regions of the Old and New Worlds as independent centres of domestication, with several more proposed. In the Fertile Crescent of southwest Asia, people were intensively managing wild cereals by about 12,000 calibrated years before present (cal BP), but non-shattering, domesticated cereal ears are not well established until about 10,500 cal BP; sheep, goats, pigs and cattle came under management between about 11,000 and 10,000 cal BP. In northern China, common millet was stored at Cishan, Hebei, from about 10,300 cal BP; in the Lower Yangtze, rice phytoliths at Shangshan, Zhejiang, show domestication beginning by about 9,400 cal BP. Maize was being processed at Xihuatoxtla shelter in Mexico's Central Balsas Valley by 8,700 cal BP. In the Andean foothills of northern Peru, people at Ñanchoc were eating squash, peanuts and beans by about 8,600 cal BP. At Kuk in highland New Guinea, cultivation mounds for bananas, taro and yam date to about 7,000–6,400 years ago. In eastern North America, local squash, sunflower, marshelder and chenopod were domesticated between about 5,000 and 3,700 cal BP, and fully domesticated pearl millet appears in southeastern Mali by about 2500 BCE.

The process was slow: in wheat, barley and rice the non-shattering trait took roughly 2,000–4,000 years to become fixed. Its causes are disputed. Climate change, population pressure and competitive feasting have all been proposed, and many researchers now doubt that any single cause explains every centre.

uncertainty.note: Start = intensified management of wild plants in the Fertile Crescent, 'at least' c. 12,000 cal BP (Zeder 2008); Larson et al. (2014) place the beginning of domestication 12,000–11,000 years ago. End is a convention: the latest primary centre dated in this record (chenopod in eastern North America, c. 3,700 cal BP intercept, Smith 2006); Larson et al. note that most domesticates arose in the middle Holocene, 7,000–4,000 BP, and domestication of new species has never fully stopped. Conversion: year = 1950 − cal BP.

how: There was no single sequence, but the best-studied centres share a pattern. (1) Foragers began to manage wild resources intensively: in the Fertile Crescent, wild cereal management goes back at least to about 12,000 cal BP, and Larson and colleagues describe a phase of predomestication cultivation documented in the Near East, China and northwestern South America. (2) Repeated sowing and harvesting selected for traits useful to people, above all ears that do not shatter; in wheat, barley and rice that trait took roughly 2,000–4,000 years to become fixed, and claims of domestication within 100–200 years have been questioned. (3) Animal management grew out of hunting strategies: in the Fertile Crescent sheep and goats were managed from about 11,000–10,500 cal BP, pigs from 10,500–10,000 and cattle from 11,000–10,000, but clear changes in bone size appear only around 9,500–9,000 cal BP. (4) Crops and herds then combined into mixed farming economies, which crystallised in the Fertile Crescent around 9,500–9,000 cal BP and spread with colonists to Cyprus (10,500–9,000 cal BP), the Aegean (9,000–8,000), Italy (c. 8,000) and the coasts of Iberia (7,700–7,300). Elsewhere the order differed: in the Americas crops were domesticated before animals, while in parts of Africa, Arabia and India animals came first. The triggers proposed include the end of the Younger Dryas cold, dry interval at about 11,700 years ago and the more stable Holocene that followed, population growth, and feasting, for which Göbekli Tepe offers evidence on a large scale.
why_it_matters: Farming changed how many people the land could feed and how they lived. A farming family typically raised more children than a foraging one, and mixed crop-and-livestock economies supported dense, year-round settlements: Çatalhöyük in Anatolia held perhaps 3,500–8,000 people at its peak in the 7th millennium BCE. The plants and animals domesticated in this period, among them wheat, barley, rice, millets, maize, squash, bananas, taro, sheep, goats, pigs and cattle, are still farmed today. Farming also spread people: colonist farmers carried the Neolithic way of life from southwest Asia to Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Iberia over about three thousand years, while Late Mesolithic forager populations there declined. The change had costs. At Çatalhöyük in Anatolia, crowding, poor sanitation and starchy diets brought infections, tooth decay and more interpersonal violence, and researchers see similar health costs in early farming societies worldwide, although a 2023 study found that much of the decline in human stature began before farming. Because farming arose independently at least eleven times, its story is not only about southwest Asia: the bananas and taro of New Guinea and the millets of the Sahel were domesticated by their own people. Had people everywhere remained foragers, human numbers would have stayed smaller and settlement more mobile, and the permanent villages on which later towns and cities were built would not have existed in the same form.

perspectives.holder: V. Gordon Childe (1934; Man Makes Himself, 1936), as summarised by Frieman (2020)
perspectives.account: Farming was a revolution comparable to the Industrial Revolution: a sudden economic change that began with grain cultivation in Mesopotamia and spread outward, transforming each society it reached.

Domestication was protracted and plural: crops were domesticated many times in at least 11 regions, cultivation of wild plants preceded visible domestication by centuries to millennia, and key traits took 2,000–4,000 years to fix, so the change was not a single sudden event.

perspectives.holder: Larson et al. (2014); Lu et al. (2009)
perspectives.account: Climate change is the main ecological backdrop: lower late-Pleistocene CO2 and temperatures limited plant productivity, and Holocene conditions made agriculture a more favourable strategy; in northern China a drier early Holocene may have favoured common millet.

perspectives.holder: Regattieri et al. (2025), from a Kurdistan speleothem record
perspectives.account: Climate cannot be used deterministically: the Zagros was largely unoccupied in the drier Younger Dryas, and permanent settlement appeared near its end, but neolithization there reworked earlier forager traditions once conditions stabilised.

perspectives.holder: Göbekli Tepe excavators (Dietrich, Heun, Notroff, Schmidt, Zarnkow 2012), building on Hayden's feasting model
perspectives.account: Large ritual gatherings and feasts among hunter-gatherers demanded food, and perhaps beer from wild cereals, which may have encouraged cereal cultivation near Karacadağ; the authors note that brewing at the site is not yet proven.

perspectives.holder: Shavit and Sharon (2023); Larson et al. (2014)
perspectives.account: Single-cause explanations (climate, population growth, technology, property or a cognitive shift) are unsatisfying; different causes may have operated in different centres.
Farming and dense settlement carried clear health costs worldwide: at Çatalhöyük, infection, dental caries, heavier workloads and interpersonal violence accompanied crowding and cereal-rich diets.

perspectives.holder: Stock et al. (2023), stature of 3,507 skeletons from 366 sites
perspectives.account: Declining stature and body mass mostly began before agriculture, mean stature bottomed out between 8,000 and 6,000 years ago, and regions of local domestication such as the Levant and China were relatively stable, so farming alone does not explain shrinking bodies.
